intro: “Must” and “have to” both express obligation (something is necessary). In positive sentences they often mean almost the same, but the feeling and the grammar are different: must is a modal verb that never changes, have to works like a normal verb.
objectifs: Form must + base verb and have to / has to + base verb correctly.
Tell the difference between the speaker's own obligation (must) and an outside obligation (have to).
Talk about obligation in the past (had to) and the future (will have to).
Ask about obligation with “Do I have to…?”.

texte: “Must” is a modal verb: it does not change with the subject (no -s) and it is followed directly by the base verb, without to.
Questions with must (“Must I…?”) exist but sound formal or old-fashioned; we almost always say “Do I have to…?”. The negative mustn't has a special meaning: see lesson 55.
exemples: I must call my mother tonight.

texte: “Have to” works like a normal verb: has to for he / she / it, and do / does / did in questions and negatives.
In spoken British English, you also hear “have got to” (I've got to go) with the same meaning, especially for one particular obligation.

lignes: positive
subject + have to / has to + base
She has to work on Saturdays.
question
Do / Does + subject + have to + base?
Do we have to pay now?
short answer
Yes, you do. / No, you don't.
Does he have to come? — Yes, he does.
past
subject + had to + base
I had to wait for an hour.
future
subject + will have to + base
You'll have to take a taxi.

sections.titre: The difference: who makes the obligation?
texte: “Must” often shows an obligation that comes from the speaker: their opinion, a personal decision, or a rule they make. It is also common in written rules and signs.
“Have to” usually shows an outside obligation: a law, a rule, a boss, a timetable, a situation you don't control. In everyday conversation, have to is much more common than must.

lignes: I must stop eating so much sugar. (my decision)
I have to take my medicine twice a day. (the doctor said so)
You must visit us in Dakar! (friendly insistence)
You have to get a visa to visit Canada. (the law)
I must study tonight. (I feel it's necessary)
I have to start work at 7. (my contract)

sections.note: In many sentences both are possible and the difference is small. If you are not sure, “have to” is almost always correct in speech.

sections.titre: Past and future: only have to
texte: “Must” has no past or future form. For a past obligation use “had to”; for a future obligation use “will have to”.
Never say “I musted” or “I will must”.
exemples: We had to leave early because of the rain.
Did you have to show your passport?
You'll have to book in advance.

texte: In speech, “must” is often used to recommend something with enthusiasm: a film, a restaurant, a visit. It is not a real obligation, but very strong advice.
exemples: You must try the grilled fish in Kribi. It's delicious!

formule: must + base (never changes) · have to / has to + base · had to (past) · will have to (future)
prononciation: “must” is often weak: /məst/ or even /məs/ before a consonant (I must go /aɪ məs ˈɡəʊ/). For emphasis, say /mʌst/.
“have to” is /ˈhæf tə/ with an f sound, not v; “has to” is /ˈhæs tə/ with an s; “had to” is /ˈhæt tə/.
“have got to” often sounds like /ˈɡɒtə/ in speech: I've got to go /aɪv ˈɡɒtə ˈɡəʊ/ (sometimes written “gotta” in text messages — avoid it in writing).
In “mustn't” /ˈmʌsnt/, the first t is silent.
erreurs: must has no past form: had to.
You will have to call him.

dialogue.contexte: Jean-Paul is starting a new job in a hospital in Liège. A colleague, Nathalie, explains the rules.
lignes: Nathalie
Welcome! First, you have to wear your badge at all times.
A hospital rule: have to.
Jean-Paul
OK. Do I have to sign in when I arrive?
Question: Do I have to…?
Nathalie
Yes, you do. And you have to wash your hands before you enter each room.
Short answer: Yes, you do.
Jean-Paul
Of course. What time does my shift start?
Asking about the timetable.
Nathalie
At seven. Yesterday the new nurse had to start at six because of an emergency.
Past obligation: had to.
Jean-Paul
I see. I must buy a good alarm clock!
Personal obligation: must.
Nathalie
Ha! And you must try the cafeteria's soup. It's the best in Liège.
Recommendation: must.

mots: You have to follow the rules.
something that tells you what you must or must not do
It's the law: you must wear a helmet.
the system of official rules of a country
The staff have to wear a uniform.
special clothes that people wear at work or school
a period of work time, e.g. 7 a.m. to 3 p.m.
to write your name on a document; a notice with information
a belt in a car or plane that keeps you in your seat
You have to pay in advance.
the last time or day to finish something

exercices.titre: 1. Must, have to or has to?
exercices.consigne: Complete with must, have to or has to (sometimes more than one answer is possible).
items: My sister ___ wear a uniform at school.
has to
I ___ remember to buy bread.
must (or have to)
Students ___ arrive before 8:30.
have to (or must, in written rules)
He ___ take the bus because his car is broken.
has to
You ___ come to our wedding! We'd love to see you.
must

exercices.consigne: Change the obligation to the time in brackets, using have to.
items: I have to work late. (yesterday)
I had to work late yesterday.
She has to take an exam. (next year)
She'll have to take an exam next year.
We have to wait. (last week)
We had to wait last week.
Do you have to wear a tie? (yesterday, question)
Did you have to wear a tie yesterday?

exercices.consigne: Write the question with do / does / did + have to.
items: you / pay / now
Do you have to pay now?
she / work / on Sundays
Does she have to work on Sundays?
they / show / their passports (past)
Did they have to show their passports?
I / bring / anything
Do I have to bring anything?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: You must to be careful.
You must be careful.
She have to call the bank.
She has to call the bank.
Yesterday I must leave early.
Yesterday I had to leave early.
Does he has to come?
Does he have to come?

exercices.consigne: Write a sentence with must or have to that means the same.
items: It's necessary for me to go now.
I must go now. / I have to go now.
Is it necessary for me to book?
Do I have to book?
It was necessary for us to take a taxi.
We had to take a taxi.

exercices.consigne: Describe the obligations of your job or studies in five sentences (present, past, and one recommendation with must).
items: Model answer

I'm a bank clerk in Yaoundé. I have to start work at 7:30 and I have to wear a suit. I don't like it, but it's a rule. Last month I had to work every Saturday because a colleague was ill. If you visit Yaoundé, you must try the restaurants in Bastos!

a_retenir: must + base: never changes, no to (I must go, she must go).
have to / has to + base: changes with the subject; questions with do / does (Do I have to…?).
must = personal obligation or written rule; have to = outside obligation (law, job).
Past: had to; future: will have to (must has no past form).
You must try / see… = enthusiastic recommendation.
